newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Investors clash with Russian steel producer.
newsitem.headline: Investors clash with Russian steel producer.

text.p: A group of Western investors threatened on Thursday to take legal action unless the management at Russia's largest steel producer Novolipetsk Metal gave them representation on the board of directors.

U.S. investment bank Salomon Bros and Moscow investment bank Renaissance Capital's Sputnik Funds said their request to nominate members to the board of directors at AO Novolipetsky Metallurgichesky Kombinat (NLMK) had been turned down on Tuesday.
Officials at Novolipetsk were not available to comment on the dispute, the latest to call into question the ability of shareholders to enforce their rights over management in Russia.

"Our investors are determined to use all legal means to obtain what is due to them under Russian law -- proportional representation," Jim Dannis, managing director and head of emerging markets at Salomon Brothers, told a news conference.
Salomon Brothers represents the offshore investment fund Cambridge Capital Management (CCM), which has a 17.2 percent stake in Novolipetsk.
It has joined forces with the Sputnik Funds, a 10 percent shareholder, and ICFI (Bank MFK in Russian), part of the Uneximbank (Oneksimbank in Russian) group, which has 15 percent.
Together the minority investors, who said they acquired the shares through vouchers and secondary market purchases, own more than 40 percent of Novolipetsk.

"The...investors have a simple and clear objective -- to increase the value of the plant by implementing better management and financial policies and by increasing investment," Dannis said. "It's the only way the shareholders can build value for their investment."

Novolipetsk, located about 400 kilometers southwest of Moscow, employs 40,000 workers and is the largest steel producer in Europe. It produced nearly six million tonnes of steel in 1995 and sales were more than $2 billion, according to the investors.

Industry experts say Novolipetsk relies heavily on the London-based TransWorld Metal trading company, which sells it raw materials. Novolipetsk repays TransWorld with a finished product which is often sold at below market rates.
"Our clients believe in the long-term value of the company. We know it's a good asset," Dannis said. He said the company was probably worth many times its market capitalisation of about $250 million.

Dannis said Novolipetsk management had consistently blocked investors' attempts to get representation on the board and given no reason for its actions. It first tossed out their request for representation on a technicality last spring.

"Many investors who poured money into the Russian stock market at the beginning of the year thought this was a thing of the past," Dannis said. "We view this as a litmus test for the Russian government's policy towards foreign investment in Russia."
